text: A quantum cloud job can fail in more ways than a typical REST API call, and several of those failure modes still cost you money even though they produced no usable result. Error handling here is where a meaningful fraction of a hybrid project's real-world risk lives.

Five failure modes recur: a queue timeout that cancels the job, a device taken offline mid-queue, a job that completes only a partial shot count, a circuit that's rejected before it ever queues, and an ordinary transient network failure. They are not the same kind of problem, and they don't deserve the same response.

Here's failure mode two in a real console — a device showing OFFLINE on Amazon Braket's own devices page. Your orchestration code has to detect exactly this state and decide: retry on a different device, not the same one.

And here's where a retry decision actually reads its evidence — a real quantum task detail page. Status, shot count, where results landed. Circuit validation failures are different from all the others: that's a classical bug in your submission code, and retrying the identical invalid circuit fails identically every time.

Here's Microsoft's own real diagram of the states every job moves through — waiting, executing, and a final state of succeeded, failed, or cancelled. Once a job hits a final state, no more updates happen, and that's exactly when your orchestration layer has to make its retry decision.

And here's why getting this right matters in dollars. A job that fails twice before succeeding on real IonQ hardware wastes sixty dollars and sixty cents — and an orchestration layer with no circuit breaker can retry blindly, racking up that cost per attempt with zero visibility into the waste.
Next lesson builds the actual retry mechanism — exponential backoff with jitter — and the concrete fallback logic for when retrying stops being the right call.
